summary: Proposes a program to develop a directory service for the Internet. It reports results of a meeting in February 1989 convened to review requirements and options. It is offered for comment and not as a committed research activity.

plainLanguage.summary:
This memo is a plan rather than a specification. It asks what an Internet-wide phone book would have to do, looks at the five naming services that existed in 1989, and proposes a three-year programme to build one.

The plan was to test several candidate services side by side before committing to any of them.

subtitle: A roadmap for building a unified Internet-wide directory service.

tldr.problem: The Internet was growing fast and people could not find each other's electronic mailboxes. The existing naming services each solved a piece of the problem, and none of them covered everything.
tldr.mechanism: A two-day meeting in February 1989 set out what a white pages service would have to do, surveyed the services that already existed, and proposed a three-stage programme: field trials, then implementation, then deployment.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a proposal for comment rather than a committed activity, and it points at X.500 as the most likely basis. It is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Need for a Directory Service
sections.content:
As part of the planned growth of the Internet, in particular in support of the full science research community in the United States, an increasing need is anticipated for various sorts of directory services. The increase in the size of the community served by the Internet and the burgeoning demands for electronic mail lead to the need for a service to find people's computer mailboxes and other relevant facts, a so-called white pages service. At the user level to date there had been no such national or international white pages service in general use. As part of building the National Research Network it was important that such a service exist, not only within that community but also crossing the boundaries into the more global network community.

Also important and related is a so-called yellow pages service, which permits the location of Internet resources based on their attributes. A white pages service is one in which one can look up people in order to learn information about them for finding them. In its simplest form it provides what the white pages telephone book provides: based on a name, one can find an address and a telephone number. In a network environment there may be many other kinds of location information, such as electronic mailbox, electronic calendar or file server, where one might leave a file for the recipient. The electronic white pages may also support a much more sophisticated set of mechanisms for lookup, matching on a more complex set of attributes than first and last name, and the searching might span more than one local white pages service.

There are a number of partial solutions to the directory service problem. Examples are the Internet Domain Naming Service, Clearinghouse, the DECnet Network Architecture Naming Service, Profile and X.500. The Domain Naming Service provides a directory service most commonly used for host naming and mail delivery. Clearinghouse and DNANS are respectively the Xerox and DEC corporate naming services, originally for mail delivery. Profile is part of the work of Larry Peterson to explore descriptive naming in a non-hierarchical structure. There is also a CCITT recommendation X.500, which defines a general directory service and whose one of its primary goals is the naming service needed for message handling. While X.500 was still developing and would need further evolution to cover all the requirements of a service for the Internet, it would have an important impact, forming the basis of commercial products and almost certainly the directory service of many parts of the network world, which implies a need to interoperate at a minimum.

In this context a meeting was held to review current requirements and solutions for directory services. For two days, a group representing academic, commercial and government interests discussed alternative candidates for a white pages service and the issues in building any such service. By the conclusion of the second day a consensus was reached on how one could achieve a white pages service in three years.
sections.plainLanguage: The email boom created a job that the phone book used to do: find a person, get their contact details. The Internet had several partial answers and no agreed one.

sections.title: What a White Pages Service Must Do
sections.content:
The requirements listed are these. Functionality: the simple form is straightforward: one should be able to query the service with the name of a person and have returned attributes of the person such as network mail address and phone number. Correctness of information: the information in a white pages service is useless and untrusted if it is not updated regularly, and the service will not be used if the information it provides is out of date or incorrect. This requires a set of management tools, and data integrity is an especially difficult challenge in this area, in contrast with information that is syntactically correct. Size: the science and research community has been estimated at ten million users, and the number of organizations in the United States is on the order of ten to one hundred thousand.

Usage and query rate: compared with the typical telephone book pattern of about one lookup a week per person, users of electronic mail in the science and research community will send more electronic mail messages than they currently make phone calls, leading to an estimate of ten searches a week per user. This leads to a query rate of 10**8 queries per week, or 170 per second on average, with much higher peak rates. The average could probably be handled by a single server, but not the peak rates, and that would leave little room for growth. A distributed, multiple server solution is therefore the only one that makes sense.

Response time: the issue arises when queries, in particular searches, are not limited to tightly constrained sets of entries. Since the number of queries generated will be proportional to the number of users and the size of the system, the design must avoid costs per query that are related to the size of the system, or the consequence will be quadratic behavior in response time. A phone book style query must respond in the waiting time tolerable to a user, perhaps ten seconds maximum, or one second desirable.

Partitioned authority: the service would be used by a wide variety of organizations, and many would find it unacceptable to delegate the authority over their namespaces to some other organization, so partitioned authority including some access control, name assignment and information management must be possible. Access control falls into two categories, read access control and write or modify access control. Read access control is needed because organizations may require limiting access to the actual entries or parts of them, comparable to organizations not being willing to distribute their corporate phone books or personnel records, and because some organizations do not want to publicize their organizational structure. Write and modify access control is necessary because both individuals and organizations may want to prevent inadvertent or malicious creation or modification of information.

Multiple transport protocol support: within the next three years one cannot expect all the organizations in the United States to convert to the OSI protocols, and some will, so it is important that any white pages service provide interfaces on top of both OSI protocols and TCP/IP. A partial OSI suite known as ISODE runs on top of TCP and is being distributed widely enough that it should probably be supported too.
sections.plainLanguage: The list mixes the obvious with the hard. Finding someone by name is easy. Keeping the records accurate, keeping the answer under ten seconds when there are ten million people, and letting each organisation control its own part of the tree are the difficult parts.

sections.title: The Services That Already Exist
sections.content:
The memo surveys the naming services that had been proposed or implemented for naming people. Implementations of all of them existed, although some were still only experimental.

The Internet Domain Name Service is used today to name host machines. It was implemented to address the query rates and database sizes consistent with looking up hosts as part of mail delivery, and it provides a hierarchy with delegation of authority within the hierarchy. Aliases are also available. There is no access control, and the service is widely distributed throughout the Internet. It supports management of distribution, replication and caching, it is operational, and it provides a rich base of practical experience. It was originally intended to be extensible to cover naming of people, and it runs on a variety of operating systems using TCP/IP.

The DECnet Network Architecture Naming Service is a rather well developed specification for a naming service that is part of the DECnet architecture. It addresses some problems not yet covered by X.500, such as access control, replication and caching, and it was explicitly defined to have great scalability and management features. It provides a global hierarchy of names which are mapped into properties, so operations of searching based on properties or attributes may be expensive and difficult. At present it is only implemented on VMS using the DNA protocols.

Clearinghouse is part of the Xerox network environment and operates today as a global service for Xerox, with considerable experience of its operation, including problems of scale. It provides a three-level hierarchy of names that are mapped to sets of properties, and loose consistency is provided through slow propagation of updates.

Profile, a project at the University of Arizona, supports descriptive naming and sophisticated lookup tools. It assumes the existence of some other service such as the DNS to navigate among Profile servers, but that navigation service need not restrict the relationship among Profile servers to a hierarchical organization, since Profile supports a non-hierarchical global structure. Names in Profile consist of sets of attributes, the largest site currently contains about 10,000 entries, and the implementation is UNIX-based only and uses TCP.

X.500 is the CCITT recommendation for a directory service. Because it is a CCITT recommendation it evolves in four year study periods, so it has a stable definition for the next four years. The set of all objects forms a single hierarchy, with each object named relative to its parent and a single root as the topmost parent. An object consists of a set of attributes, and searching can be done by a logical combination of attribute values, known as a filter. The hierarchy as described is geographic at its top level and organizational within that. X.500 is distributed, specifying cooperating servers, Directory Server Agents, under local control and management, each knowing about one or more parts of the hierarchy; the clients are Directory User Agents. It is defined to run on top of the OSI protocol stack, and the Internet demonstrations run on top of ISODE, which provides OSI transport on top of TCP.

X.500 is incomplete in that there are identifiable areas where the standard says nothing but need to be specified for a successful implementation, such as access control, replication, caching, the shape of the hierarchy, tools to limit the scope and cost of searching, and database management tools. Several implementations were in progress, including the Quipu project at University College London, and Quipu is probably the most complete implementation to date: its pilot version had about 20 Directory User Agents in seven countries with an estimated 20,000 entries in total.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the five solved a different part. The DNS was the most widely deployed but had no access control. X.500 was the international standard but was missing several things a working service needs.

sections.title: The Three-Stage Plan
sections.content:
The conclusion of the report is that some form of X.500 is the most likely candidate, because it has a rich semantics and will become the international de facto standard. There are, however, serious problems with its incompleteness and with its strict hierarchy. To explore these and become convinced of its viability, the attendees agreed on field trials as a first stage. This would include experiments with at least one X.500 implementation, Quipu, Profile to explore a non-hierarchical structure and richer descriptive naming, and DNANS to explore some of the incomplete aspects of X.500 for which DNANS has architected solutions.

A three-stage plan, with all three stages beginning coincidentally and as soon as possible, would provide such a service within the National Research Network. The first stage should be complete in a year, the second in two, and the third in three. Stage 1 would be field trials of three approaches to naming, with an emphasis on distinguishing between the specification and a particular implementation of X.500. Stage 2 would be a more complete implementation of a white pages service based on the conclusions from Stage 1. Stage 3 would be widespread deployment of the implementation developed in Stage 2. If the field trials were to lead to the conclusion that none of the services is adequate, the plan for the remainder of the work would need to be rescheduled.

The group also identified the major projects needed to undertake the programme: further implementation of code for the field trials, since each of Quipu, Profile and DNANS would need to be modified to utilise the common file format into which the input data about users would be gathered; design, development and evaluation of user interfaces; design and development of data gathering and management tools; oversight and evaluation of the field trials, which must produce a document that is both a general specification and profiling information for later interoperability and conformance testing; detailed planning and later management of deployment, including delegation of authority over parts of the namespace and arbitrating the shape of the namespace; standards participation, which the group said could take up to one half of one person's time in a year; and a task force or working group to provide a forum for communication and discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Three stages of a year each, all starting at once: try the candidates, build the winner, then roll it out. The reasoning was that acting now would produce a coherent solution before a plethora of ad hoc ones appeared.

sections.title: What the Field Trials Would Have to Settle
sections.content:
Field trials would be valuable for two reasons. The software is still in early stages of development or deployment, some of it production code but still a first release and the rest part of research projects. And it is important to learn from experience with a limited and sympathetic community, the suggested community being computer science departments, with the NASA and Department of Energy community recommended for the DNANS experiments. A single common file format for storage of and access to the naming information, and a single set of data management tools, was recommended, so that the services could be co-resident, share files and permit direct comparisons.

The issues the trials would have to resolve are listed in the memo. On functionality, X.500 and DNANS make strong statements about the organization of the namespace, both being a single, absolute hierarchy with soft links or aliases and attribute-based naming. Profile provides a more general facility that supports any form of relative names, not just hierarchical, and a small programming language to express search functions.

On size, a white pages service must be prepared to handle a minimum of 10**7 entries and a query rate of hundreds per second, with much higher peak rates, and the response time for Directory User Agents must be reasonable for a human at a console. The trials must allow experimentation under stressful conditions, with both large and small nodes and both heavy and light load querying, and must be able to test reorganization such as moving a piece of the hierarchy and handling naming conflicts in the new environment, which X.500 does not address.

On distribution, replication and caching, X.500 has very little to say, while a great deal of work has been done in the DNS and DNANS. Replication is necessary for accessibility in a large-scale or global namespace, and again X.500 does not address it. Caching is barely touched on in X.500 and not at all in Profile, but the memo's experience with the DNS indicates that caching is critical to effective operation of a distributed name service.

On access control, accountability and integrity, X.500 supports authentication based on an RSA public key algorithm but does not address universal registration, access control or accountability themselves. Profile does not address these issues either, although it uses UNIX authentication. DNANS takes a strong stand on access control, architecting it at the level of individual entries.

On the structure of the naming tree, the memo notes that in the deployment of the DNS about one year was lost to arguments about the actual structure of the naming hierarchy, and that the same issue will arise here. The problem is made harder because the hierarchy will be global, and X.500 is an international standard based on the assumption that there is only one example of the tree, partitioned by country. Specific issues include how delegation of control of the tree is managed and how the creation of new parts of the tree is controlled. Support for tree search matters because the X.500 naming hierarchy can be expected to become very large, and users need help finding their way to unknown parts of the namespace, for which a consistent policy for the use of alias entries is needed. Definition of database structures, meaning the schema defining attributes and object classes, must also be specified. Load balancing requires estimating the dynamic performance of the system so that servers can be sized properly, especially at the root of the tree. Finally, supporting multiple protocol suites matters because at least three are and will continue to be used in that environment, DECnet, TCP/IP and the OSI suite, and since the white pages service is at the applications layer it must run on top of at least these three.
sections.plainLanguage: The trials were meant to find the gaps: the things X.500 did not say, such as caching, replication and who is allowed to change a record, and the things it said in a way that might not work, such as insisting on one global tree.

viz.caption: The three stages of the proposed programme

items.title: Stage 1: field trials, one year
items.text: Run X.500, Profile and DNANS side by side with a common file format, to tell apart gaps in the X.500 specification and gaps in one implementation of it.

items.title: Stage 2: implementation, two years
items.text: Build a production quality service on the conclusions of the trials, with reliable servers and a variety of clients for people and for programs.

items.title: Stage 3: deployment, three years
items.text: Gather and manage the information, place the servers, distribute and train users on the client code, and delegate authority over the contents.
